newsitem.title: DUBAI: Americans in Saudi on alert a year after bomb.
newsitem.headline: Americans in Saudi on alert a year after bomb.

text.p: Americans in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday marked the first anniversary of a bomb attack on U.S. servicemen still on alert for further "terrorist" action.
Callers to a U.S. embassy security hotline in Riyadh were cautioned that the anniversary could provide an excuse for "terrorist" groups to attack U.S. interests or facilities.
Five Americans and two Indians were killed in the car bomb at a Saudi National Guard training centre in the heart of the Saudi capital on November 13, 1995.

An executioner in May publicly beheaded four Saudis who had confessed on television to their roles in the blast. They said they were influenced by militant Islamists opposed to the presence of foreign forces in the homeland of Islam.
Three weeks later, a much larger fuel truck packed with explosives killed 19 American airmen and wounded about 400 at a barracks in the eastern city of Khobar.

U.S. and other Western forces deployed in the Gulf stiffened security, including the relocation of thousands of U.S. Air Force servicemen to a remote desert base 100 km (60 miles) southeast of Riyadh, where extra security was enforced.
American, British and French air forces patrol a "no-fly zone" over southern Iraq from bases in Saudi Arabia.

The U.S. embassy message, recorded last week, told callers: "The embassy and Saudi security will continue to work closely to enhance the safety of Americans." A U.S. spokesman said it was not triggered by any threat being received by the embassy.
About 40,000 Americans, 5,000 of them military, live in Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Interior Minister Prince Nayef said on Monday that Saudi Arabia was determined to fight terrorism and ready to cooperate with any country for that purpose.
"We in the kingdom will fight terrorism," he said at the end of a meeting of Gulf Arab interior ministers in the Omani capital Muscat.
Saudi Arabia would cooperate with "any country that wants to cooperate with us...in exchanging information or cooperating over security matters".
"The United States is concerned with this because the victims of the two bombings in Khobar and Riyadh were American citizens," he added.

U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation agents have been in the kingdom since shortly after the blast but there has been controversy over the level of cooperation they receive from Saudi security authorities.
FBI agents have privately expressed frustration at what they called a lack of Saudi cooperation. The FBI has denied U.S. reports that it was withdrawing its agents.
The Washington Post reported recently that Saudi authorities had arrested 40 Saudis in connection with the second blast and were convinced Iran backed a broad conspiracy in the attack.

Tehran rejected the charges as "a new U.S. conspiracy to create internal conflict in Islamic-Arabic countries" and Prince Nayef played down the report, saying Saudi security officials were the only credible source of news.
"Nothing can be said (about the case) unless it is by the Saudi security sources. And that will be the truth," he said.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, who made several visits to Saudi Arabia after the second bomb, said on November 1 Washington had not yet determined who was behind the blast.
Perry said he had pressed Saudi authorities to cooperate.
